sections.title: Understanding the Problem
points: The app records runs and rides from GPS samples. Users can view their completed activities and their friends' activities.
The device must continue recording without network access. Cloud synchronization must not interrupt the athlete's local display.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
points: Users can start, pause, resume, stop, and save an activity.
The app displays route, distance, and active time during the activity.
Users can view completed activities. Live sharing and distance leaderboards are extensions in the deep dives.

sections.title: Non-functional Requirements
points: Recording must work offline. Local persistence limits data loss after the app or device stops unexpectedly.
The interview scenario supports ten million concurrent activities.
Local statistics must remain responsive. The design balances sample frequency, battery use, network traffic, and durable storage.

sections.title: Core Entities
points: User identifies the athlete. Activity records its type, start time, state changes, distance, and duration.
Route contains timestamped GPS coordinates for an activity. Sequence identifiers can make repeated uploads safe.
Friend connects users who share activities. Leaderboard records aggregate an athlete's completed distance by activity type and applicable filters.

sections.title: API
points: POST /activities creates an activity. PATCH /activities/:id records state changes, including COMPLETE.
The route endpoint accepts timestamped locations. The offline design sends accumulated samples, with chunks for a very large route.
GET /activities lists personal or friends' completed activities with pagination. GET /activities/:id returns full details.
Optional endpoints return live activity updates and distance rankings. Live viewers can poll for changes.

sections.title: 1) Record and display activity
points: The initial client creates an activity through the Activity Server. Each state change records a status and timestamp.
The initial route path sends periodic GPS samples to the server. The server stores them and updates distance.
The server stores activity metadata and route coordinates separately. The offline deep dive moves immediate calculations onto the device.
Sample timestamps preserve the recorded route. Status intervals distinguish active time from pauses and total elapsed time.

diagrams.caption: Users should be able to start, pause, stop, and save their runs and rides.
While running or cycling, users should be able to view activity data, including route, distance, and time.

flows.title: Record through the initial server-based path
steps: The client creates an activity through the Activity Server. The server returns its activity ID.
The client samples GPS coordinates at the configured interval. It includes the original sample timestamp in each upload.
The Activity Server stores route points and updates distance from successive coordinates.
Pause and resume requests append timestamped state changes. The duration calculation excludes paused intervals.
The client sends COMPLETE when the athlete saves the activity. The offline deep dive reduces these frequent network requests.

sections.title: 2) Read completed activities
points: Saving the activity changes its state to COMPLETE. The initial design already holds its route and summary data.
The Activity Server lists completed activities for the requested user or their friends. The first response contains only summary fields.
A detail request returns the selected activity and route. The client draws the route using the stored coordinates.

diagrams.caption: Users should be able to view details about their own completed activities as well as the activities of their friends.

flows.title: Read a saved activity
steps: The client requests personal or friends' activities from the Activity Server.
The server queries completed activities for the permitted user IDs. It returns a page of summaries.
The user selects an activity. The client requests that activity by ID.
The server returns the full route and activity details. The client draws the route and displays its metrics.

sections.title: 1) Offline operation
points: The phone buffers GPS samples and calculates local statistics. It periodically saves the buffer to persistent device storage.
After reconnection, it uploads retained samples. Stable sample or batch identifiers prevent repeated uploads from duplicating data.
The device records pause and resume events. A gap in network uploads does not by itself mean that movement stopped.
The phone removes local data only after the server confirms storage. Partial uploads remain recoverable until finalization succeeds.

diagrams.caption: How can we support tracking activities while offline?

flows.title: Record locally and synchronize after reconnection
steps: The phone samples GPS data and updates its local route, distance, and active time.
It appends samples and state changes to an in-memory buffer. It periodically persists that buffer on the device.
After an app restart, the phone restores the saved buffer before recording additional data.
When connected, it sends the completed activity or accumulated batches to the Activity Server.
The server stores the samples and state changes. Stable identifiers prevent duplicate data from repeated uploads.
After the server confirms durable storage, the phone removes the acknowledged local data.

sections.title: 2) High write volume
points: Uploading a completed activity greatly reduces requests compared with sending every GPS sample. Very large uploads can use chunks.
The source keeps a simple Activity Server and database. Horizontal server scaling handles additional CPU, memory, or network demand.
Completion-time partitions support recent-activity queries. The partition scheme must also avoid concentrating all current writes on one overloaded shard.
Recent activity data can use a cache. Older route data can move to cheaper storage when lower access speed is acceptable.

diagrams.caption: How can we scale to support 10 million concurrent activities?

sections.title: 3) Live sharing
points: The athlete's device sends updates every few seconds while retaining local recording. Friends poll at a similar interval.
A small display buffer smooths movement between updates. It adds a deliberate delay while reducing abrupt location changes.
SSE or WebSockets are alternatives when tighter latency is required. Reporting frequency still affects battery use and server load.

sections.title: 4) Leaderboards
points: This article ranks athletes by total completed distance. A periodic job can group activities by user and store aggregate totals.
Redis sorted sets provide a faster alternative for maintained totals. Separate sets can represent activity types and countries.
Arbitrary time ranges still require filtering and aggregation, or precomputed time windows. Retry-safe updates and durable activities support ranking rebuilds.

flows.title: Build periodic distance rankings
steps: A scheduled job reads newly completed activities for the selected activity type and period.
It groups distances by athlete and applies the requested geographic filters.
It stores the resulting per-athlete totals in the leaderboard table.
A leaderboard request reads and orders those totals. New activities appear after the next aggregation run.

flows.title: Maintain a Redis distance leaderboard
steps: The Activity Server commits a completed activity to durable storage.
The ranking update checks whether that activity already affected the relevant total.
It adds the distance to the athlete's applicable global and country-specific Redis sorted-set scores.
A ranking request reads the appropriate set. Arbitrary time ranges require their own aggregation or precomputed windows.
A cache rebuild derives totals from durable activities. Replayed updates must not count an activity twice.

sections.title: Final Design
points: The phone records locally and uploads completed activity data. The Activity Server writes durable metadata and routes.
The database partitions and archives activity data as needed. Redis maintains frequently requested distance leaderboards.
Optional live polling operates alongside local recording. A failed live update must not stop recording or later synchronization.
